title: Welcome talk for new university students

lines.t: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Hartley University. My name is Dr Nora Finch, and I am the head of student support.
I know many of you are nervous today, so I will keep this short and practical.
I will talk about four things: your cards, the library, your timetable, and where to find help.
First, your student cards. Some of you have already queued at the main office, but that is not where you collect them.
Cards are issued at the Student Hub, in the old chapel building.
Please bring your passport or national identity card, and the letter confirming your place.
The photo will be taken on the spot, so there is no need to bring one.
Second, the library. It opens at eight in the morning and closes at ten at night on weekdays. At weekends it closes at six.
Sorry, I should say five on Sundays, because the staff finish early.
During the exam period in May, the ground floor stays open all night. Please do not bring hot food inside, but drinks with a lid are fine.
Third, your timetable. It appears in your online account from Friday. Do not worry if two classes seem to overlap.
This happens in the first week because some groups are still being finalised, and you will receive an email by Monday evening with the corrected version.
Fourth, getting help. Many students wait until they are in real difficulty before asking. Please do not do that.
Our advisers can help with money problems, health, housing and study skills.
You can book an appointment online, or simply walk in between ten and one on Tuesdays and Thursdays.
There is also a free writing clinic, which I strongly recommend if you have never written an academic essay.
One last thing. Tomorrow at two o'clock there will be a campus tour starting outside the library.
Actually, we have moved it to half past two, because the sports hall needs the earlier slot.
The tour lasts about forty minutes, and you will finish at the student café, where your first coffee is free.
Enjoy your first week, and remember that every student here started exactly where you are now.

qs.why: البطاقات تُصدر في مركز الطلبة وليس في المكتب الرئيسي.

qs.why: سيصل بريد إلكتروني بالجدول المصحح مساء الاثنين.

qs.why: الإرشاد دون موعد: الثلاثاء والخميس من العاشرة إلى الواحدة.

qs.why: تم تأخير الجولة إلى الثانية والنصف.

lines.t: This is the Tuesday morning community report, and today I am in the town of Millbrook, where a small recycling scheme has become a big success.
The scheme began eighteen months ago with just four hundred households. Today more than two thousand three hundred families take part, which is roughly half the town.
The idea is simple. Each home has three bins. Blue is for paper and cardboard, green is for glass, and yellow is for cans and hard plastics.
Food scraps go into a small brown container collected every week.
Organiser Maria Lopez told me the early months were difficult.
Nearly a third of what people put in the bins could not be recycled at all, because it was dirty or in the wrong bin.
To fix that, the scheme trained forty volunteers, called street champions. Each one visits a few neighbours, explains the rules, and answers questions over a cup of tea.
The result is striking. The share of unusable waste has fallen from thirty percent to just nine percent.
There is also a reward system. Households collect points for every bag they recycle correctly.
At first the plan was to pay cash, but residents voted instead for vouchers to spend in local shops, and that has helped small businesses on the high street.
Money is being saved, too. Because less rubbish goes to landfill, the town pays lower fees, and the council says it saved about sixty thousand dollars last year.
All of that has gone into a new playground by the river.
Of course, not everyone is happy. Some residents complain that thin plastic film, like the wrapping on magazines, is still not accepted.
Maria says the machines at the sorting plant simply cannot handle it, but she is searching for a company that can.
The next step is the apartment blocks, which have shared bins and so have been harder to include.
Maria hopes to start in the spring, with the first building on Oak Street.
Reporting from Millbrook, I'm Jenna Walsh. Back to the studio.

lines.t: Hello, everyone, and welcome to the Riverside Science Museum. My name is Tom, and for the next forty-five minutes I will be your guide.
Before we begin, a few practical points. Large bags must go in the lockers by the entrance.
You need a two-dollar coin, but do not worry, you get it back when you open the locker again.
Photography is welcome everywhere except the planetarium. You may use your phone, but please switch off the flash, because it can damage some of our older exhibits.
Let us start here in the entrance hall. The tall swinging weight above you is a pendulum, nine metres long.
As the Earth turns, the pendulum slowly knocks down the small wooden blocks on the floor, one about every fifteen minutes.
Behind me is the Energy Hall on the ground floor.
You can pedal a bicycle to light up a model city, and you will quickly discover how hard it is to power even one street.
On the first floor you will find the Human Body gallery. The most popular exhibit is a giant model of the heart that you can walk through.
Visitors often tell me they never realised how loud it is inside.
The second floor has two attractions. One is the Space gallery, with a real meteorite you may touch.
The other is the planetarium, where there are two shows each day, at eleven fifteen and again at half past twelve.
Sorry, I mean at twelve forty-five, since we changed the schedule this month.
Children under ten must be with an adult in the experiment lab, which is also on the second floor.
Today's experiment is making slime, which is always a favourite.
When you are tired, head to the café on the top floor.
It has wonderful views of the river, but it closes at four, an hour before the museum itself.
The lifts are at the back of the building, past the gift shop. If you have any questions, please just ask me.
Now, if you would follow me to the Energy Hall.

qs.why: طول البندول تسعة أمتار.

qs.why: المقهى يُغلق في الرابعة، قبل المتحف بساعة.

title: A new working from home policy

lines.t: Good afternoon, everyone. Thank you for joining this call. I want to explain our new working from home policy, which begins on the first of March.
First, the background. For two years we have allowed home working on a case by case basis.
That led to confusion and, frankly, some unfairness, so we are replacing it with one clear policy.
The basic rule is this. Everyone may work from home for up to two days a week. The other three days are spent in the office.
To make sure teams can meet, Tuesdays and Thursdays are fixed office days for everybody.
We first considered Mondays and Thursdays, but the data showed far fewer people travel in on Mondays.
When you work from home, you should be online and reachable between ten and four. Outside these core hours, you can organise your day as you wish.
Now, equipment. The company will provide a laptop and a second screen, and you may take them home.
We will also pay a one-off allowance of a hundred and fifty pounds towards a proper chair or desk. You will need to send us the receipt.
We did discuss paying part of your broadband bill. In the end, finance decided it was too complicated to administer, so that will not be included.
Please remember security. Always use the company VPN, and avoid working on confidential files in cafés or on public wifi.
To apply, log in to the HR portal and choose your two days. Your line manager has five working days to approve or comment.
Most requests will be accepted, unless the nature of your job needs you on site, as with the reception team and the laboratory staff.
New employees can use the policy only after their three-month probation period ends.
Finally, this is a six-month trial. In the fourth month we will send a short survey, and we will decide in September whether to make the policy permanent.
If you have questions, email me or visit the HR page. Thank you.

qs.why: حتى يومين في الأسبوع.

title: A talk for legal advice centre volunteers

lines.t: Welcome, everyone, and thank you for volunteering at the Eastside Legal Advice Centre. I am Rachel Moore, the volunteer coordinator.
Let me begin with the most important point. Volunteers do not give legal advice, not even simple advice, and not even if you are a law student.
Only our qualified lawyers do that. Your role is to help people reach them.
In practice, you will greet clients at reception, check their identity, and complete an intake form with their basic details and the nature of their problem.
You will also tell them how long they are likely to wait, which is usually about forty minutes.
About forty percent of our clients come with housing problems, such as unfair rent increases or a landlord refusing to repair something.
The next biggest group, around a quarter, have employment problems, mostly unpaid wages.
Many clients are frightened or embarrassed when they arrive, so please be patient. If someone becomes very upset or angry, do not argue.
Stay calm and call your supervisor.
Confidentiality is essential. Before your first shift you will sign an agreement.
You must never discuss a client's situation outside the centre, even without using their name, and you must not put private details in emails.
We also help people who do not speak English well.
We have a telephone interpreting service for more than thirty languages, so please never ask a family member or child to translate.
Now, the practical details. The centre is open Monday to Thursday from nine to five, and we run a free clinic on Saturday mornings.
Each shift lasts four hours.
We ask volunteers to commit to at least six months. I originally planned three, but training takes time, and clients benefit from familiar faces.
Training consists of two evening sessions. The first is next Tuesday at six o'clock in the meeting room upstairs.
You will receive an identity badge then, so there is no need to dress formally. Smart casual is fine.
Any questions before we begin the first session?
